processing: Shaded before picking, then steamed. It goes mainly into tencha, the unrolled leaf that is ground into matcha, and also into rolled gyokuro.
harvest_season: Mid-season spring, about the same as Yabukita or up to two days later.
appearance_dry: As gyokuro, fine and tightly twisted with a bright sheen; as tencha, even, soft flakes with a bright lustrous colour.
appearance_liquor: Typical of shaded Kyoto gyokuro: a clear pale green-yellow.
appearance_wet: Thin, soft, pale green leaves with a slightly wavy outline.
taste_profile: Shading brings out a pleasant seaweed-like aroma; expect the rich umami and low bitterness usual for gyokuro and tencha cultivars.

brewing.notes: Settings for gyokuro. If you have it as matcha, whisk it instead and ignore the timings.

vintage_note: Most of it disappears into blended matcha and gyokuro, so single-cultivar lots are uncommon. As with other shaded Japanese teas, it is sold from the current spring's harvest, and tencha is typically ground close to sale. Check the grind or packing date on matcha.
description:
Ujihikari is a Kyoto cultivar made for shaded tea. It comes from a selection of Uji plants, and in Kyoto it is one of the main plants behind tencha, the raw leaf of matcha, as well as gyokuro.

The leaf explains why it is valued. The shoots are slightly small, thin and pale, with a distinctive wavy shape, and they make tencha that is even and soft with a bright colour. Under shade they pick up a pleasant marine aroma.

Detailed notes on its taste as a single cultivar are rare. Expect what shaded Uji tea usually offers: umami and sweetness with little bitterness. For gyokuro, use cool water and a small pot; for matcha, sift and whisk.

It yields less than Yabukita and is somewhat sensitive to cold, so it stays a specialist plant. If a Kyoto shop names it, that is a good chance to taste the cultivar on its own.
history: The Kyoto Prefectural Tea Research Institute bred Ujihikari from Uji stock under the line name Kyoken 170 and completed it in 1954. It has not been nationally registered, but it is fairly common in Kyoto Prefecture, where it is grown alongside Asahi and Samidori for tencha.
